name: APTOS thread lift

card.summary: A non-surgical lift using barbed non-absorbable threads placed under the skin; early series report improvement, while case reports document migration and expulsion.
card.note: Wikipedia cites a BBC investigation reporting short training courses for practitioners; complications such as thread migration have been reported.

quick.overview:
APTOS threads are barbed polypropylene sutures inserted under facial skin to support sagging tissue without a surgical facelift. They are typically promoted for the cheeks, jowls and jawline and form part of the broader thread-lift category.

Early reports from the originator's group describe improvement in contour in a series of 186 patients. Later literature includes case reports of complications and small retrospective studies of combined treatments.
quick.mechanism: Sharp dents or barbs along each thread grip the tissue; the thread is anchored so that it holds the tissue in a higher position. Some authors describe stimulating tissue response around the thread as well.
quick.risks: Reported problems include thread migration and partial expulsion; a MACS facelift has been used to correct APTOS complications. Wikipedia notes that UK practitioners face no mandatory qualification and cites a physician quoted by the BBC describing thread lifts as potentially causing irreversible damage.

lead: APTOS threads are barbed non-absorbable sutures, originally made of polypropylene with dents along their length, used to lift ptotic facial tissue without a facelift.[1] The technique was described in 2002 by a group who used them in 186 patients and reported success in lifting various areas and improving facial contour.[1]

A 2004 review describes self-retaining barbed sutures as innovations for nonsurgical facial and neck rejuvenation available as short APTOS threads or long WOFFLES threads; its author uses APTOS for malar rounding and firming and WOFFLES as a sling to temporal scalp tissue.[2] A 2005 chapter describes the approach as the featherlift.[3]

Complications are documented in case literature, including thread migration and partial expulsion.[4] Wikipedia notes that UK aesthetic practitioners need no mandatory qualification and reports a BBC investigation of short low-cost training courses.[5] Evidence is mainly case series and retrospective studies, plus small registered trials without published results found.

People seeking a firmer jawline or fuller, higher cheeks use thread lifts as a lower-downtime alternative to a facelift. Surgeons contrast this with the traditional facelift, which reshapes deeper facial layers by dissection and can last years longer, while threads are placed through small entry points without removing skin.[14]

paras: The original APTOS sutures were polypropylene threads modified with many dents along their length so the sharp edges hold tissue firmly.[1] Short threads are used for areas such as the cheeks, while longer threads act as slings anchored to firm tissue.[2] More recent products include absorbable poly-L-lactic acid and polycaprolactone threads.[7]

The facelift itself dates to the early twentieth century: Eugen Holländer reported one in Berlin in 1901, and the field moved from skin-only pulling to deeper-layer techniques after Tord Skoog's subfacial dissection in 1968, the description of the SMAS layer in 1976 and Paul Tessier's subperiosteal work in 1979.[5] Thread lifting grew out of the wish for a lift without that surgery. The APTOS method (the name refers to anti-ptosis) was published in 2002 by its developers, and by 2004 and 2005 surgeons were describing short APTOS threads, long WOFFLES sling threads and a combined approach called the featherlift.[1][2][3]

Reports describe using APTOS threads for malar rounding, facial tightening, jawline and marionette line correction (with a collagen-stimulating filler),[2][8] and, in a 2025 retrospective study, non-surgical otoplasty.[9] A 2026 paper describes a suture-crossing technique for contour restoration.[7]

A 2005 case report described migration and partial expulsion of an Aptos thread after initially successful fixation.[4] A 2012 report used a MACS lift and fat grafting to treat a complication from APTOS sutures.[6] Wikipedia describes a BBC report quoting a physician who called thread lifts among the most dangerous aesthetic procedures, with possible irreversible damage.[5]

Because non-absorbable threads stay in the tissue, an error in placement can persist; the Wikipedia article on thread lifts quotes a physician describing thread lifts as potentially causing irreversible damage, and reports that a BBC undercover recording of a short training course showed poor infection control.[14] It also reports that the BBC counted 26 cosmetic training academies in Liverpool in 2021, with courses from a few hours online to a few days in person.[14]

Within aesthetic practice, threads are discussed as a way to tighten the lower face and define the jaw. A 2022 prospective chart review of 50 patients (mean age about 54) combined APTOS threads with a collagen-stimulating filler to treat the jawline, jaw angle and marionette lines, and reported satisfaction rising from 74% at six months to 86% at twelve months.[8] The same literature describes threads used alongside energy devices and fillers, and the Wikipedia article on thread lifts notes that combining threads with other rejuvenation methods may give better results.[14]

APTOS stands for anti-ptosis, and the technique rests on the barbs or dents cut into the thread. Once the thread is passed under the skin, those projections catch the subcutaneous tissue, and the thread is anchored so the tissue is held in a higher position, which is what gives the visual lift of a sagging cheek or jowl without removing skin.[1][14] Wikipedia describes the threads as barbs that pull tissue upward without excision and notes that the threads are non-absorbable.[14]

Thread length changes the use. The 2004 review describes short APTOS threads used for cheek rounding and firming, and longer WOFFLES threads used as a sling to suspend tissue from firmer anchoring tissue in the temporal scalp.[2] The featherlift described in 2005 is the name given to facial lifting with APTOS threads as a minimally invasive procedure.[3]

Facelift surgery, which dates to Eugen Holländer's 1901 report, reshapes deeper layers by dissection and is generally described as longer-lasting than threads, whereas thread lifts are placed through small entry points with less downtime.[5][14] Reported adjuncts include collagen-stimulating fillers for jawline and jaw-angle work, microfocused ultrasound (examined in a registered trial of thread lifting plus ultrasound for face tightening) and fat grafting.[8][11][6]

Clinicians also describe other uses of the same thread: a 2025 retrospective study of 250 patients reported non-surgical ear reshaping with an APTOS kit, and a 2024 case report used APTOS barbed sutures in chronic facial paralysis.[9][13]

The 2002 series of 186 patients is the founding report and was authored by the technique's developers.[1] Registered trials include a completed study of HA-coated versus non-HA threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction (n=144)[10] and a study combining thread lifting and microfocused ultrasound (n=45, status unknown).[11] No published results from these were found. No randomized trials establishing longevity were found.

A 2026 retrospective survey in a private aesthetic practice invited 159 patients treated between 2024 and 2026; 97 gave complete numeric answers. Mean overall satisfaction was 8.7 out of 10, 81% rated satisfaction at 8 or higher, and about a quarter had had other facial procedures alongside the threads.[12]

A retrospective study from Amman, Jordan covered 250 patients (500 ears) aged 7 to 67 who had non-surgical otoplasty with an APTOS kit under local anesthesia, with satisfaction and adverse events recorded through EAR-Q questionnaires.[9] A 2024 case report described using non-absorbable APTOS threads to improve facial symmetry in a patient with chronic facial nerve paralysis.[13] These are single-centre observational reports rather than randomized comparisons.

In the UK, practitioners who perform thread lifts are not required to hold a mandatory qualification, according to Wikipedia's account of the BBC reporting.[14] The same reporting quotes a physician who described the procedure as among the most dangerous in aesthetics when done by under-trained practitioners.[14]

chain: Barbed thread is placed under the skin
Barbs grip soft tissue and hold it higher
Cheek, jowl and jawline contour is repositioned without surgical excision
angle.text: APTOS threads are used to reposition sagging cheek, jowl and jawline tissue, giving a lifted facial contour without a facelift incision. Reports describe satisfaction rising over the months after treatment, particularly when threads are combined with a filler or other treatments.
